seasons.review_body: The Scarecrow aired on ENA from April 20 to May 26, 2026, and turned into the network's all-time top-rated Monday-Tuesday drama through sustained word-of-mouth rather than an opening burst. Premiere ratings sat at 2.9 percent nationwide before climbing steadily to a finale peak of 8.1 percent. The show is built around collective guilt and institutional violence rather than the mechanics of whodunit: a demoted detective and a former school bully turned prosecutor are forced to investigate serial murders inspired by the real Hwaseong case, and the series keeps asking who the system destroyed before the killer. Park Hae-soo and Lee Hee-joon - reunited from Mouse - deliver performances that critics called emotionally shattering. K-waves and Beyond labelled it a crime thriller that keeps breaking the viewer's heart, and the MyDramaList audience consensus of 8.2 validated that assessment.

episode_reviews.title: Tae-ju's Comeback to Gangseong
episode_reviews.review_body:
# The Scarecrow S01E01: "Tae-ju's Comeback to Gangseong" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

The confession arrives before the case is ready for it. **Lee Seong Jin** is brought into the cell, the countdown keeps moving, and fear does the work evidence has not done. By the time he says, "I... I killed her, sir," the episode has already made its sharpest move: it gives the investigators the answer they wanted, then starts making that answer look dangerous. This pilot is about procedure eating its own tail. The system wants closure. The facts refuse to sit still.

## A Confession Built to Crack

The hour's central trick is simple and effective: it treats a confession as an event, then strips away its comfort. **Detective Kang** begins from familiar crime-pilot ground. He wants the serial murders tied down. The case needs a name, the room needs a suspect, and the pressure needs somewhere to land. The early explanation that **Lee Yong Woo** has remained in prison since his life sentence gives the episode its procedural baseline. The past has a locked door around it.

That makes Seong Jin's arc sharper. He enters the interrogation dynamic trying to survive the accusation, not steer the case. The countdown beat matters because it turns the scene into a machine. Time is made visible. His begging for help is pressure producing a result, and the direction understands the difference. The confession lands as a win for the room and a warning for the episode.

The writing's best instinct is to avoid celebrating that confession. It knows a procedural shortcut when it sees one. Seong Jin gives the case what it wants, but the episode has already taught the audience to be wary of clean answers. That is where the pilot earns its confidence: the first big solution functions like bait.

It also gives Kang an immediate problem. If he accepts the confession too quickly, he becomes another part of the machinery that pushed Seong Jin into speaking. If he resists it, he has to admit the investigation may be less stable than his own team needs it to be. That tension is stronger than simple doubt. It turns the confession from a plot point into a test of method.

## Corruption Walks in Through the Side Door

The arrest of **Sergeant Choi Jeong Mo** for taking bribes gives the pilot a second engine. Placing a bribery arrest near the start changes the temperature around every later interrogation. Authority enters the room compromised. The question from the public-disruption stretch, "Which option is going to be worse for the Commissioner?", pins the rot to consequence rather than mood. Someone's arrest becomes someone else's political problem.

That thread helps the episode avoid becoming a one-room pressure exercise too early. The public ceremony disruption, with its spike in dialogue density, gives the hour a messy civic surface before the interrogation tightens everything into fear. The line about an empty seat being no big deal sets a confrontational rhythm. People in this world do not whisper their conflicts into corners. They push them into rooms where rank, embarrassment, and leverage can be seen.

The corruption material also widens the meaning of the central case. If cops, commissioners, and prosecutors are all reading the murders through institutional pressure, then no answer arrives clean. A suspect can be useful before he is proven guilty. A confession can solve a headline before it solves a crime. The pilot keeps returning to that danger without turning every official into a cartoon villain.

The cost is focus. The corruption beat matters, but the hour asks the audience to juggle institutional embarrassment, serial-murder framing, and suspect pressure before its cleanest dramatic shape arrives. The clutter has purpose, yet it still slows the front half. The pilot is stronger when evidence fights confession directly.

## The Alibi Turns the Knife

The strongest reversal lands when the investigator claims Lee Seong Jin was in lockup when a key victim was murdered. That is the pilot's proper snap. It does more than question the confession's reliability. It attacks the case's timeline, which is a colder weapon. A frightened man can lie. A broken suspect can confess. A lockup record is harder to sentimentalize.

This is where Detective Kang becomes more interesting than a standard confession hunter. His internal contradiction is the episode's lead performance on the page: he wants a confession for the serial murders, then ends up arguing Seong Jin is not the real killer. That turn gives him a practical morality. He is no saint walking into a corrupt system. He is a cop whose desired result collides with a fact too large to ignore.

The episode also uses this pivot to widen the serial pattern. If there are four victims rather than two serial victims, the case cannot remain a tidy package. The open question grows sharper: who benefits when the pattern is framed narrowly? That is strong pilot construction because it makes the mystery procedural before it makes it mythic. The scarecrow connection is planted, but the episode keeps it as a hook instead of explaining it into dust.

The timing of the alibi matters as much as the information. By placing it late, the episode lets the audience feel how quickly an investigation can harden around a preferred story. Seong Jin's confession has already taken up space in the room. People have reacted to it. Careers and assumptions have begun arranging themselves around it. Then the timeline cuts through all of that. One fact makes the room look foolish.

That is the pilot at its best. It trusts the mechanics of the case to create dread. No speech about truth is needed. The record does the damage.

## Cha Si Yeong Draws the Line

**Prosecutor Cha Si Yeong** enters the hour as the figure most committed to evidence and prosecutorial control. Her role is not soft counsel. She questions direct evidence, warns against weakness, and forces the case to move by proof rather than appetite. That makes her closing warning to Kang land cleanly: "Det. Kang, I'm a Prosecutor first, and your friend second."

It is a good final-position line because it reframes allegiance without overplaying betrayal. Friendship exists, but it does not run the case. Procedure does. Cha's insistence gives the pilot its spine: emotion may start an investigation, pressure may produce a confession, but the file still has to survive contact with evidence. A weaker version of this hour would treat the confession as the big cliffhanger. Here, the more interesting question is whether the people inside the system can stop themselves from using the wrong answer because it is convenient.

Cha also gives Kang a necessary counterweight. His urgency is understandable, especially with the murders pressing in and the case demanding movement. Her resistance keeps that urgency from becoming the episode's moral center by default. She does not need to be warmer to be right. The episode understands that professional distance can be its own form of care when the alternative is a bad case built fast.

Still, Cha's edges are clearer than her interior in this opener. The episode defines her through function: prosecutor first, friend second, evidence above weakness. That works for a pilot juggling several case strands, but the character will need more than institutional steel if the season wants her conflict with Kang to carry emotional weight. The final line gives her position. Future episodes need to give her cost.

## The Verdict

"Tae-ju's Comeback to Gangseong" is a sturdy, tense procedural opener with one strong structural idea: the first confession is treated as a problem, not a prize. The episode is at its best when Detective Kang's need for closure crashes into the lockup timeline and forces the case away from easy certainty. The bribery arrest and public confrontation add institutional grime, though the front half spreads its attention wider than the drama can fully sharpen.

The pilot works because it keeps turning answers into liabilities. Seong Jin's confession should simplify the case, but it exposes the danger of wanting simplicity too much. Kang's certainty gives him momentum, then the timeline forces him to change course. Cha's warning gives that change a professional boundary. The scarecrow thread remains just visible enough to promise a larger pattern without drowning the opener in mythology.

BollyAI's score: 7.4/10. As a season starter, it plants clean questions about the true killer, the victim count, and the scarecrow warning while giving the central investigation a solid procedural spine.

episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere establishes the atmosphere of institutional rot before the first murder scene: a detective demoted to his provincial hometown, a cold case that local powers want buried, and a prosecutorial adversary with a shared past. The show withholds easy genre comfort from the first episode.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Tae-joo's first confrontation with Si-young reveals their shared history carries as much danger as any serial killer in the town.

verdict.one_liner: A tense pilot where the first confession solves nothing, and that refusal to settle becomes the hour's smartest weapon.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 12
episode_reviews.review_body: The Scarecrow Season 1 Episode 12 aired May 26, 2026 on ENA as the series finale. The episode peaked at 9.3 percent nationwide minute-by-minute ratings, confirming how completely the show had grown its audience from a 2.9% premiere. K-waves and Beyond called the series 'disturbing yet brilliant' and noted that 'the mystery stops being who did this and becomes: how many lives were destroyed before the truth came out.' The finale delivers on that thematic promise: the resolution refuses to let the institutions that enabled the murders escape without indictment, making the closing hour a statement about collective complicity rather than individual evil. Park Hae-soo and Lee Hee-joon's final confrontation with the true forces behind the murders reframes every earlier scene of authority and compliance. The show's graduation from 2.9% to 9.3% across twelve episodes is itself the story of what word-of-mouth can do when content earns it.
